claims.claim: The indispensable material factor in the generation of power is the living together of people, and whoever isolates himself forfeits power and becomes impotent.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The only indispensable material factor in the generation of power is the living together of people. Only where men live so close together that the potentialities of action are always present can power remain with them, and the foundation of cities, which as city-states have remained paradigmatic for all Western political organization, is therefore indeed the most important material prerequisite for power. What keeps people together after the fleeting moment of action has passed (what we today call “organization”) and what, at the same time, they keep alive through remaining together is power. And whoever, for whatever reasons, isolates himself and does not partake in such being together, forfeits power and becomes impotent, no matter how great his strength and how valid his reasons.

claims.claim: Tyranny rests on isolation and contradicts the essential human condition of plurality, generating impotence rather than power.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Montesquieu realized that the outstanding characteristic of tyranny was that it rested on isolation—on the isolation of the tyrant from his subjects and the isolation of the subjects from each other through mutual fear and suspicion—and hence that tyranny was not one form of government among others but contradicted the essential human condition of plurality, the acting and speaking together, which is the condition of all forms of political organization.

definitions.definition: What keeps people together after the fleeting moment of action has passed, dependent upon the unreliable and only temporary agreement of many wills and intentions, and corresponding to the condition of plurality.
An indivisible human attribute tied to the bodily existence and production of things, which is checked by the presence of others and helpless against power.
That which one man alone can exert against his fellow men, associated with the monopoly of the means of violence; it can destroy power but never become a substitute for it.

distinctions.distinction: Power depends upon the being together and agreement of many and can be divided without decreasing, whereas strength is indivisible, tied to bodily existence, and represents an individual capacity for producing things.
Power relies on human plurality and agreement, whereas force can be exerted by a single individual or a few through violence and can destroy power without ever substituting for it.

must_not_be_lost: The definition of power as generated by human togetherness and plurality rather than individual strength or force.
Montesquieu's insight that tyranny rests on isolation, contradicts plurality, and necessarily generates impotence.
output.segment_function: Explication of power, its dependence on human plurality and living together, its distinction from strength and force, and its relation to tyranny.
